The Detroit Pistons are an American professional basketball team based in Detroit.
The Pistons compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the Central Division of the Eastern Conference.
The team plays its home games at Little Caesars Arena, located in Midtown Detroit.
The Detroit Pistons were founded as the Fort Wayne Zollner Pistons in 1937.
The Fort Wayne Zollner Pistons turned professional in 1941 and joined the National Basketball League (NBL).
The Fort Wayne Zollner Pistons won two NBL championships: in 1944 and 1945.
The Fort Wayne Zollner Pistons also won the World Professional Basketball Tournament in 1944, 1945, and 1946.
In 1948, the team became the Fort Wayne Pistons and joined the Basketball Association of America (BAA).
The NBL and BAA merged to become the NBA in 1949, and the Fort Wayne Pistons became part of the merged league.
In 1957, the franchise moved to Detroit.
The Detroit Pistons have won three NBA championships: in 1989, 1990, and 2004.
Fred Zollner owned the Zollner Corporation, a foundry that manufactured pistons for car, truck, and locomotive engines in Fort Wayne, Indiana.
In 1937, Fred Zollner sponsored a semi-professional company basketball team called the Fort Wayne Zollner Pistons after receiving a request from his workers.
The Fort Wayne Zollner Pistons shed their works team roots and joined the National Basketball League (NBL) in 1941.
There are suggestions that Pistons players conspired with gamblers to shave points and throw various games during the 1953–54 and 1954–55 seasons.
In particular, there are accusations that the team may have intentionally lost the 1955 NBA Finals to the Syracuse Nationals.
Dave Bing joined the team in 1966, scoring 1,601 points in his rookie year.
Fort Wayne's small size made it difficult for the Pistons to be profitable as other early NBA teams based in smaller cities started folding or relocating to larger markets.
After the 1956–57 season, Fred Zollner decided that Fort Wayne was too small to support an NBA team and announced the team would be playing elsewhere in the coming season.
Fred Zollner ultimately settled on Detroit as the new location for the Pistons.

Detroit had not seen professional basketball in a decade due to losing the Detroit Eagles due to World War II, both the Detroit Gems of the NBL (who became the Minneapolis Lakers) and the Detroit Falcons of the BAA in 1947, and the Detroit Vagabond Kings in 1949.
Fred Zollner decided to keep the Pistons name as it made sense given Detroit's status as the center of the automobile industry.
George Yardley set the NBA single-season scoring record in the Pistons' first season in Detroit by becoming the first player to score 2,000 points in a season.
The Pistons played in Olympia Stadium for their first four seasons and then moved to Cobo Arena beginning in the 1961–62 season.

During the 1960s and 1970s, the Pistons were characterized by talented players including George Yardley, Bailey Howell, Dave Debusschere, Dave Bing, and Bob Lanier, questionable trades, and frequent coaching changes.
Debusschere was the youngest player-coach in the history of the NBA at one point.
A trade during the 1968–69 season sent DeBusschere to the New York Knicks for Howard Komives and Walt Bellamy.
DeBusschere became a key player in leading the Knicks to two NBA titles.
Howell had previously been dealt to the Baltimore Bullets in 1964, and former Pistons guard Gene Shue assessed the Pistons as having the worst management in the league at the time.
Yardley, Lanier, and Bing all ended their Pistons tenure being traded away, frustrated with the direction and opportunities with Detroit.
In 1974, Zollner sold the team to glass magnate Bill Davidson, who remained the team's principal owner until his death in 2009.

The Pistons had a winning season in 1971 after spending the 1960s below .500 and then had a brief period of sustained success in the mid-1970s, qualifying for the playoffs in four straight seasons (1974, 1975, 1976, and 1977).
Hope was placed in Dick Vitale in 1978 as the former head coach at the University of Detroit, but he was fired the following season.

The Pistons limped into the 1980s with a 16–66 record in 1979–80 and lost their last 14 games of the season which, when coupled with the seven losses at the start of the 1980–81 season, constituted a then-NBA record losing streak of 21 games.
The Pistons acquired point guard Isiah Thomas from Indiana University in November 1981 and Vinnie Johnson from the Seattle SuperSonics in a trade in November 1981.
In February 1982, the Pistons acquired center Bill Laimbeer from the Cleveland Cavaliers.
Another key move by the Pistons was hiring head coach Chuck Daly in 1983.
The Pistons lost a tough five-game series to the underdog New York Knicks in 1984.
In the 1985 playoffs, Detroit won its first-round series and faced the defending champion Boston Celtics in the conference semifinals but were defeated by Boston in six games.

Isiah Thomas scored an NBA Finals record 25 points in the third quarter while playing on a severely sprained ankle in Game 6 of the 1988 NBA Finals against the Los Angeles Lakers, who won the game and the series.
The Pistons won their first NBA championship in 1989 by defeating the Los Angeles Lakers in four games. Joe Dumars was named NBA Finals MVP.
The Pistons successfully defended their title in 1990 despite losing Rick Mahorn to the Minnesota Timberwolves in the expansion draft.
In 1993, Isiah Thomas suffered a wrist injury that affected his performance during the playoffs.

The Pistons were swept by the Chicago Bulls in four games in the 1991 Eastern Conference Finals and walked off the court without shaking hands with the Bulls after Game 4 due to comments made by Michael Jordan.
After getting swept by the Bulls, the Pistons traded James Edwards and waived Vinnie Johnson during the off-season.
The Pistons finished the 1993–94 season with a 20–62 record.
Following the 1993–94 season, they drafted Grant Hill with the third overall pick in the 1995 NBA draft.
Joe Dumars was hired as the team's president of basketball operations after retiring following the 1998–99 season.
Grant Hill elected to leave for the Orlando Magic but was traded back to the Pistons along with Ben Wallace and Chucky Atkins from Orlando in exchange for Hill.
The Pistons finished the 2004 NBA Finals with a 54–28 record, recording their best record since 1997.
In the 2003 Eastern Conference Finals, the Pistons were swept by the New Jersey Nets in four games.
Larry Brown coached the Pistons to the 2004 NBA title and the Eastern Conference championship the following season.
The Pistons suffered through another tough season in 2000–01, going 32–50 despite Jerry Stackhouse averaging 29.8 points a game.
After the 2000 playoffs, Joe Dumars was hired as the team's president of basketball operations.
Grant Hill played only 47 games in the following three seasons due to a recurring ankle injury.
The Pistons won their first 50-win season since 1997 and their first playoff series victory since 1991 by defeating the Toronto Raptors in five games during the 2003 playoffs.
In the 2004 playoffs, after defeating the Milwaukee Bucks in five games, they defeated the defending Eastern Conference champion New Jersey Nets in seven games after coming back from a 3–2 deficit.
The Pistons then defeated the Pacers, coached by Rick Carlisle, in six tough games to advance to the NBA Finals for the first time since 1990.
In the 2004 NBA Finals, the Pistons defeated Los Angeles in five games for their third NBA championship. Chauncey Billups was named NBA Finals MVP.
The Pistons posted double-digit wins in three of their four victories and held the Lakers to a franchise-low 68 points in Game 3 during the 2004 NBA Finals.
Despite losing key members of their bench during the off-season, the Pistons were considered a strong contender to win a second consecutive title in 2005.
The Pistons won 54 games during the regular season and advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals for the fifth consecutive season but were defeated by Miami Heat in six games.
During the 2007 NBA draft, the Pistons selected Rodney Stuckey with the 15th overall pick and Arron Afflalo with the 27th overall pick.
They also re-signed Chauncey Billups to a long-term contract, as well as top prospect Amir Johnson and key reserve Antonio McDyess.
The Pistons selected Rasheed Wallace in the February 2004 trade. He developed into a defensive stalwart in the coming years.
The Pistons finished the season with a record of 64–18, setting new franchise records for both overall and road victories (27) during the 2005–06 season.

The Pistons opened the 2007 NBA playoffs with a 4–0 victory over the Orlando Magic. The team advanced to face the Chicago Bulls in the Eastern Conference Finals but were eliminated by Miami Heat in six games.

In the 2008 NBA playoffs, Detroit started out poorly with a Game 1 loss to the seventh-seeded Philadelphia 76ers and found themselves in a 2–1 deficit. However, they rallied to defeat the Sixers in six games.
The Pistons faced the Orlando Magic in the semifinals but lost badly in Game 3, 111–86, and lost all-star point guard Chauncey Billups to a hamstring injury.
Despite his absence, the Pistons won Game 4 on a field goal by Tayshaun Prince with just 8.9 seconds to play, taking a 3–1 series lead.
The Pistons then proceeded to win Game 5 in Detroit and won the series 4–1.
Detroit advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals for the sixth straight season but lost to the Celtics in six games.
On June 3, 2008, the Pistons announced that Flip Saunders would not return as head coach.
The Pistons hired Michael Curry to be their new head coach on November 3, 2008.
On November 10, 2008, Antonio McDyess was waived and rejoined the Pistons on December 9.
The Pistons traded key members Chauncey Billups and Antonio McDyess to the Denver Nuggets for Allen Iverson on November 3, 2008.
Iverson signed with the Memphis Grizzlies during the off-season.

In the off-season, the Pistons reached an agreement with former Chicago Bulls guard Ben Gordon on a five-year/$55 million contract and an agreement with former Milwaukee Bucks forward Charlie Villanueva on a five-year contract worth $35 million.
The Pistons lost their two key members during the last few years, veterans Rasheed Wallace and Antonio McDyess.
On July 8, 2009, the Pistons hired former Cavaliers assistant coach John Kuester to be the new head coach.
The Pistons re-signed Ben Wallace on August 12, 2009.
Despite these changes, the team regressed even further, as they were hampered by setbacks and injuries.
On March 23, 2010, the Pistons were eliminated from playoff contention with a loss to the Indiana Pacers. The Pistons finished with a 27–55 record, their worst since 1994.
Another 50-loss season, this time finishing at 30–52, led to the firing of Kuester at the end of the 2010–11 season.
On June 10, 2011, Karen Davidson reached a long-awaited agreement to sell the franchise to billionaire Tom Gores.
The deal also included The Palace of Auburn Hills and DTE Energy Music Theatre. According to Crain's Detroit Business, the final sale price was $325 million.
In the 2011 NBA draft, the Pistons selected Brandon Knight, Kyle Singler, and Vernon Macklin.
Prior to the start of the 2011–12 season, Dennis Mannion was appointed as president of the franchise and Palace Sports & Entertainment. Lawrence Frank was hired as the head coach.
The 2011–12 season saw an improvement for the Pistons but they still posted a losing record.
The team continued to build its young core with the drafting of the talented center Andre Drummond.

Following the 2012–13 season, Frank was fired on April 18, 2013. Maurice Cheeks was hired as head coach and president of basketball operations but lasted only half a season before being replaced by interim coach John Loyer.
In April, Joe Dumars stepped down as president of basketball operations but remained as an advisor to the organization and its ownership team.
Stan Van Gundy was hired on May 14, 2014. He signed a five-year, $35 million contract to become the head coach and president of basketball operations for the team.
The Pistons started the 2014–15 season with a 5–23 record but waived Josh Smith in the summer of 2013.
The team went on a lengthy winning streak but finished the season with a record of only 32–50 after Brandon Jennings' Achilles injury.
In the 2015 off-season, Pistons head coach Stan Van Gundy began to change the roster by making such acquisitions as Ersan İlyasova, Marcus Morris, Aron Baynes, and Steve Blake.
They also drafted rookie Stanley Johnson with the eighth pick in the 2015 NBA draft and re-signed point guard Reggie Jackson.
Andre Drummond started the season strong, earning consecutive Eastern Conference Player of the Week awards for the weeks of November 1 and 8.
The Pistons entered the All-Star break at 27–27. They surpassed their win totals from the 2009–10 season to the 2014–15 season on March 9, 2016.

On April 6, 2016, following a 108–104 win over the Orlando Magic, the Pistons reached 42 wins and were assured their first winning season since the 2007–08 season. On April 8, 2016, they defeated the Washington Wizards 112–99 and clinched a playoff berth for the first time since 2009.
The Pistons faced the top-seeded Cleveland Cavaliers in the first round of the 2016 NBA playoffs but were swept in four games.

On November 22, 2016, the Pistons officially announced their intention to move to Little Caesars Arena and the site of The Palace of Auburn Hills was to be redeveloped and sold. The arena likely would be demolished as part of the redevelopment.
The Pistons ended their 39-year stay in Oakland County when they moved to Little Caesars Arena starting with the 2017–18 season.
On June 20, 2017, Detroit City Council approved the Pistons' move to Little Caesars Arena. On August 3, 2017, the NBA Board of Governors unanimously approved the move, making it official.

The Pistons announced they had acquired all-star forward Blake Griffin along with Willie Reed and Brice Johnson from the Los Angeles Clippers in exchange for Avery Bradley, Tobias Harris, Boban Marjanovic, a 2018 first-round draft pick, and a 2019 second-round draft pick on January 29, 2018.
The Pistons finished the 2017–18 season with a 39–43 record. They missed the playoffs for the eighth time in ten years.
On May 7, 2018, the Pistons announced that Stan Van Gundy would not return as head coach and president of basketball operations.
Dwane Casey was hired by the Pistons to be their new head coach on June 11, 2018. He agreed to a five-year deal.
The Pistons finished the 2018–19 season with a 41–41 record, clinching a playoff spot as the eighth seed in the Eastern Conference.
In the first round of the 2019 NBA playoffs, the Pistons were swept by the Milwaukee Bucks in four games, setting an NBA record for the most consecutive playoff losses with 14.

On March 11, 2020, the 2019–20 season was suspended after it was reported that Rudy Gobert tested positive for COVID-19. On June 4, 2020, the season came to an end when the NBA Board of Governors approved a plan that would restart the season with 22 teams returning to play in the NBA bubble on July 31, 2020.
The Pistons finished the season with a 20–46 record.
Cade Cunningham was selected first overall in the 2021 NBA draft. On June 18, 2020, Troy Weaver was hired as the new general manager.
The Pistons finished the 2020–21 season with the second-worst record in the league at 20–52 and missed the playoffs for a second consecutive season.
In the 2021 NBA draft, the Pistons selected Cade Cunningham first overall. The Pistons finished the 2021–22 season at 23–59 and missed the playoffs for the third consecutive season.
With the fifth overall pick in the 2022 NBA draft, the Pistons selected Jaden Ivey. Later in the first round, they acquired Jalen Duren via a trade with the New York Knicks.
The Pistons finished the 2022–23 season with the worst overall record in the NBA and third-worst in franchise history at 17–65. It was their first 60-loss season since 1993–94.
